native_result.query: How does the consideration of academic characteristics alter the effects of Socioeconomic Status and race on BA degree completion?
native_result.HypoA: When academic characteristics are considered, the effect of SES on BA degree completion is reduced and the effect of race is enlarged.
native_result.HypoB: Considering academic characteristics substantially alters the apparent effects of socioeconomic status and race on educational attainment. Using the NLSY79 data, where the outcome must be proxied by 'highest grade completed by 1979' (no explicit BA degree-completion variable exists in the file; binary sensitivity uses grade >= 13), the raw (unadjusted) associations show large race gaps - Black respondents completed on average 0.86 fewer grade levels (OR 0.56 for reaching grade 13) and Hispanic respondents 0.41 fewer (OR 0.60) than non-black/non-Hispanic peers, while family net income (1979) showed no significant association (beta ~ 0, p=0.96). After adding academic characteristics - an ASVAB composite (1981 z-scores of the four sections, beta=0.80 per SD, OR 3.37) and, in the rank subsample, class-rank percentile (beta=-0.09, p=0.02) - the Black coefficient attenuates by ~69% (-0.83 -> -0.25; OR 0.56 -> 1.11, no longer significant), the Hispanic coefficient is fully absorbed and changes sign (-0.45 -> +0.28), and the family-income coefficient emerges as significantly negative (beta 0.00 -> -0.13; OR 0.95 -> 0.80), a suppression pattern indicating that income's association with attainment runs largely through academic performance. Thus, academic characteristics are the dominant driver of attainment (R2 0.03 -> 0.15), and most of the unadjusted SES and race 'effects' are re-attributed to academic performance once it is considered. Caveats: (1) the outcome is a proxy for educational attainment measured in 1979, not actual BA degree completion; a true BA indicator (grade >= 16) has only n=39 and is unusable. (2) The academic variables (ASVAB 1981, class rank 1981) are measured AFTER the outcome year, so the attenuation is associational only and cannot be interpreted as causal mediation of BA completion. (3) Missingness is race-differential (ASVAB missing: 10.4% Black, 7.8% Hispanic, 14.1% other; rank missing: 64.0/60.0/51.6%), so complete-case estimates carry a composition bias; the Hispanic sign flip is less robust in the rank subsample (where it remains negative, -0.17), while the Black attenuation (58-69%) is consistent across both samples.
